note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Airflow 3.4.0: task loops, a draining state, and breaking defaults for Python, Postgres and asset runs
items.summary: Released on 6 November 2026. Task groups can now repeat at runtime with .loop() (an until condition and a max_iterations cap), an experimental Dag importer accepts Dags written in TypeScript, Go, Java or YAML, and a new 'draining' Dag state lets active runs finish and then pauses the Dag. Breaking: Python 3.11 or later is required, the Dataset alias is gone from the airflow module (use Asset from airflow.sdk), psycopg3 (postgresql+psycopg://) is the Postgres driver, asset-triggered Dags start one run per event instead of batching events, and try_number on an up_for_retry task now points at the next try.
items.why: Upgrades break on exactly these lines: the metadata database connection string, old Dataset imports, and Dags that assumed several asset events would be batched into one run. Loops and draining are new tools for polling patterns and safe deploys that interviewers increasingly ask about.
items.try: In projects/lakehouse/airflow/dags/lakehouse_daily.py, list every import and connection string an upgrade to 3.4 would touch, then sketch how a downstream Dag triggered by the daily table asset would behave if three events arrived in one minute (three runs now, not one) and whether its tasks are idempotent enough for that.

items.title: Snowflake Open Data Sharing is GA: share Iceberg tables with engines outside Snowflake
items.summary: On 2 November 2026 Snowflake made Open Data Sharing generally available. Consumers outside Snowflake can read live, read-only Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables through the standard Iceberg REST Catalog API, without copies or ETL, authenticating with programmatic access tokens or workload identity federation (AWS, Azure, GCP or OIDC). External consumers can be added to existing listings, and cross-region sharing works in AWS and Azure commercial regions.
items.why: Sharing used to mean the consumer also ran Snowflake (or used a reader account). Now a partner's Spark, Trino or DuckDB can read the shared table directly, which changes how you design data products and is a strong answer to 'how do two companies on different platforms share data'.
items.try: In module 8's build (the same data on two platforms), write down which tables you would expose as an Iceberg share, what identity the external engine would use, and how you would test that it can read but never write; then compare the cost and freshness with exporting Parquet files to the partner.

items.title: Snowflake backups now cover Iceberg tables on Snowflake Storage (GA on AWS)
items.summary: On 4 November 2026 backup sets gained support for Iceberg tables on Snowflake Storage (CREATE BACKUP SET ... FOR ICEBERG TABLE) and dynamic Iceberg tables, restored with CREATE [DYNAMIC] ICEBERG TABLE ... FROM BACKUP SET. Schema and database backups now include eligible Iceberg tables. Available on AWS.
items.why: Immutable backups and recovery were a reason to keep regulated data in native tables. With Iceberg tables covered, an open format no longer costs you the disaster-recovery story, which is a common objection in platform design rounds.
items.try: For the governance incident in module 8 (delete one rider everywhere), write down how a backup set interacts with the right to be forgotten: how long backups keep the deleted rider, and what retention you would set so recovery and deletion rules both hold.

items.title: Snowflake's managed MCP server can run agents in the background
items.summary: On 4 November 2026 the Snowflake-managed MCP server's CORTEX_AGENT_RUN and CODING_AGENT tools gained a background option that returns a handle the client polls. Servers with those tools automatically get ASYNC_AGENT_RUN_STATUS, ASYNC_AGENT_RUN_CANCEL and AGENT_RUN_RESULT, which do not count toward the 50-tool limit, and a content_cel_filter parameter lets a client read an outline first and fetch only the blocks it needs.
items.why: Long warehouse agent jobs no longer have to fit inside an MCP client timeout, and reading only the parts of a large result keeps the agent's context small and cheap. Start, poll, cancel and fetch is the pattern to describe for any long-running tool.
items.try: In module A4's read-only data tool lab, add a second tool pair, start_query and query_status, that returns a handle immediately and lets the agent poll, and decide what the agent does if the status never reaches done (budget, cancel and report).

items.title: Databricks: AI Function tasks in jobs (Beta), and AI Functions in SQL will need Runtime 17.3 LTS
items.summary: On 4 November 2026 Databricks added a Beta job task type that runs ai_parse_document, ai_extract or ai_classify over files in a volume or rows in a table and processes only new or changed inputs. On 5 November it announced that from January 2027 AI Functions in SQL require Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS or later (ai_similarity and the REST API are unaffected).
items.why: LLM extraction becomes an incremental, orchestrated job step, which is how it should be designed: only new inputs, retries, and cost you can see per run. Teams calling AI Functions from older runtimes have a hard upgrade date.
items.try: In module A4's AI column function lab, make your function skip rows it has already processed (keyed on a content hash), then count how many model calls a second run makes; it should be zero for unchanged rows.
